1 INDICATIONS AND USAGE Amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL is indicated for the treatment of pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years weighing less than or equal to 40 kg with: Recurrent or persistent acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae (penicillin MICs less than or equal to 2 mcg/mL), H. influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), or M. catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains) characterized by the following risk factors: Antibacterial drug exposure for acute otitis media within the preceding 3 months, and either of the following: 1) age 2 years, or younger or 2) day care attendance [see Microbiology (12.4) ] . Limitations of Use Amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL is not indicated for the treatment of acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae with penicillin MIC greater than or equal to 4 mcg/mL. Acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae alone can be treated with amoxicillin. Therapy may be instituted prior to obtaining the results from bacteriological studies when there is reason to believe the infection may involve both S . pneumoniae (penicillin MIC less than or equal to 2 mcg/mL) and the beta-lactamase-producing organisms listed above. Usage To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL and other antibacterial drugs, amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL should be used only to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility information are available, they should be considered in selecting or modifying antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may contribute to the empiric selection of therapy. Amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL is a combination of amoxicillin, a penicillin-class antibacterial and clavulanate potassium, a beta-lactamase inhibitor, indicated for the treatment of pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years weighing less than or equal to 40 kg with Recurrent or persistent acute otitis media due to S. pneumoniae (penicillin MICs less than or equal to 2 mcg/mL), H. influenzae (including beta-lactamase-producing strains), or M. catarrhalis (including beta-lactamase-producing strains) characterized by the following risk factors (1): Antibacterial exposure for acute otitis media within the preceding 3 months, and either of the following: 1) age 2 years, or younger or 2) daycare attendance. [dosage_and_administration]
2 DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION Pediatric Patients aged 3 months to 12 years weighing less than or equal to 40 kg: 90 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours, administered for 10 days. ( 2 ) 2.1 Important Administration Instructions To minimize the potential for gastrointestinal intolerance, amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL should be taken at the start of a meal. Absorption of clavulanate potassium may be enhanced when amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL is administered at the start of a meal. 2.2 Dosage in Pediatric Patients Pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years weighing less than or equal to 40 kg : Based on the amoxicillin component (600 mg/5 mL), the recommended dose of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL is 90 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours, administered for 10 days (see Table 1 as a general example guideline for attainment of this dosage). This dose provides 6.4 mg/kg/day of the clavulanic acid component. Table 1: General Dosage Guidelines for Amoxicillin and Clavulanate Potassium for Oral Suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL in Pediatric Patients Body Weight (kg) Volume of Amoxicillin and Clavulanate Potassium for Oral Suspension, ​​​​​​​600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL providing 90 mg/kg/day 8 3 mL twice daily 12 4.5 mL twice daily 16 6 mL twice daily 20 7.5 mL twice daily 24 9 mL twice daily 28 10.5 mL twice daily 32 12 mL twice daily 36 13.5 mL twice daily 40 15 mL twice daily ​​​​​​​ Pediatric patients weighing greater than 40 kg : Experience with amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL in this group is not available. 2.3 Dosage in Adult Patients Experience with amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL in adults is not available and adults who have difficulty swallowing should not be given amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL in place of the amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium 500 mg or 875 mg tablet. 2.4 Dosage in Patients with Hepatic Impairment Hepatically impaired patients should be dosed with caution and hepatic function monitored at regular intervals [see Warnings and Precautions (5.4) ]. 2.5 Preparation of the Oral Suspension Prepare the suspension at time of dispensing as follows: Tap bottle until all powder flows freely. Measure the total amount of water (see Table 2) to be added in two parts. Add approximately 2/3 of the total amount of water for reconstitution, replace cap and shake vigorously to suspend powder. Add remainder of the water (that had been measured), replace cap and again shake vigorously. Table 2: Volume of Water for Reconstituting Amoxicillin and Clavulanate Potassium for Oral Suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL Bottle Size Amount of Water Required for Reconstitution 75 mL 68 mL 125 mL 108 mL 200 mL 170 mL ​​​​​​​​​​​​​​Each 5 mL will contain 600 mg of amoxicillin as the trihydrate, and 42.9 mg of clavulanic acid as the potassium salt. Shake oral suspension well before each use. Suspension must be refrigerated. Discard after 10 days. Suspension is off-white at time of reconstitution; some color change is normal during the dosing period. Flavoring Information : For patients who wish to alter the taste of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL, immediately after reconstitution, 1 drop of FLAVORx ® (apple, banana cream, bubble gum, cherry, or watermelon flavor) may be added for every 5 mL of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL. The resulting suspension is stable for 10 days under refrigeration. Stability of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL when mixed with other flavors other than the 5 flavors listed above has not been evaluated. 2.6 Switching between Dosage Forms and between Strengths Amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL does not contain the same amount of clavulanic acid (as the potassium salt) as any of the other suspensions of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium. Amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL contains 42.9 mg of clavulanic acid per 5 mL, whereas the amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium, 200 mg/28.5 mg per 5 mL suspension contains 28.5 mg of clavulanic acid per 5 mL and the 400 mg/57 mg per 5 mL suspension contains 57 mg of clavulanic acid per 5 mL. Therefore, the amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium 200 mg/28.5 mg per 5 mL and 400 mg/57 mg per 5 mL suspensions should not be substituted for amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium for oral suspension, 600 mg/42.9 mg per 5 mL as they are not interchangeable.

user: Which other drugs interact with Amoxicillin?
response:
{"answer":"Key drugs and classes that interact with amoxicillin (and practical recommendations)

1) Probenecid
- Mechanism: reduces renal tubular secretion of penicillins → increases and prolongs amoxicillin plasma levels.
- Clinical action: interaction is sometimes used intentionally to boost levels; otherwise be aware of increased antibiotic exposure and possible adverse effects.

2) Methotrexate
- Mechanism: penicillins can reduce renal clearance of methotrexate → increased methotrexate toxicity (myelosuppression, mucositis).
- Clinical action: monitor for methotrexate toxicity and consider spacing or dose adjustment; check methotrexate levels and CBC if high‑dose methotrexate.

3) Anticoagulants (warfarin and other coumarins; also reports with direct oral anticoagulants)
- Mechanism: antibiotic therapy can alter gut flora and vitamin K production and/or affect metabolism → increased INR and bleeding risk.
- Clinical action: monitor INR closely when starting or stopping amoxicillin (especially amoxicillin/clavulanate) and adjust anticoagulant dose as needed.

4) Valproic acid / divalproex
- Mechanism: broad‑spectrum antibiotics may reduce enterohepatic recirculation of valproate → decreased serum valproate levels and risk of breakthrough seizures.
- Clinical action: monitor valproate levels and clinical seizure control; consider alternative antibiotic if high seizure risk.

5) Allopurinol
- Mechanism/issue: concomitant allopurinol plus aminopenicillins (e.g., ampicillin/amoxicillin) has been associated with an increased incidence of rash.
- Clinical action: counsel patient about rash risk; consider alternatives if history of allopurinol rash or severe reactions.

6) Oral contraceptives (estrogens/progestin pills)
- Mechanism: possible reduction in enterohepatic recirculation of estrogen by antibiotics may lower plasma estrogen levels (clinical significance debated and uncommon).
- Clinical action: advise patients to use backup contraception while taking amoxicillin and for a short interval after finishing therapy if concerned.

7) Aminoglycosides
- Mechanism: inactivation can occur if mixed in the same IV solution; penicillins can be antagonistic in vitro although they are commonly used together clinically for synergy against some organisms.
- Clinical action: do not mix amoxicillin and aminoglycosides in the same IV bag/line; time dosing appropriately and monitor renal function when used concomitantly.

8) Tetracyclines and other bacteriostatic antibiotics
- Mechanism: bacteriostatic drugs (tetracyclines, chloramphenicol) may antagonize beta‑lactam bactericidal activity in some situations.
- Clinical action: avoid combinations when bactericidal activity is critical, or use with clinical rationale; consider alternative regimens.

9) Mycophenolate mofetil / mycophenolic acid
- Mechanism: broad‑spectrum antibiotics can alter gut flora and reduce enterohepatic recirculation of mycophenolic acid → decreased exposure and potential risk of rejection in transplant patients.
- Clinical action: consider monitoring mycophenolate levels (if available) or clinical markers, and consult transplant team for adjustments.

10) Live oral bacterial vaccines (e.g., oral typhoid)
- Mechanism: antibiotics can reduce replication/efficacy of live oral bacterial vaccines.
- Clinical action: avoid administering live oral bacterial vaccines concurrently with antibiotics; delay vaccination until antibiotic course is completed and gut flora recovered.

Other practical notes
- Renal impairment or concomitant nephrotoxic drugs: amoxicillin is renally excreted; adjust dosing for severe renal dysfunction and monitor when combined with nephrotoxic agents.
- Hepatic impairment: for amoxicillin/clavulanate formulations, monitor hepatic function (clavulanate component implicated in cholestatic hepatitis).

This is not an exhaustive list. If you have a specific concomitant medication in mind, tell me the drug and I will give tailored interaction detail and recommended management."}
